We all know there are countless consequences attributed to climate change. One that sticks in my head in particular is flooding. Many gorgeous islands like the Maldives or Tuvalu are under threat of being completely flooded and destroyed in the coming few decades, if climate change remains on its current course. Even countries way closer to home like the Netherlands are under threat of flooding. 

Even though we live in a comparatively less affected country, the effects can and will hit us eventually and partly already have. Extraordinarily hot summers have ravaged through Switzerland in the last few years, posing a risk to fires and to the dying of crops. But also very wet summers have caused landslides and floods already. 

In summary, it is extremely important to combat climate change, as not doing so will result in countless deaths and, for the rest of us, harsh lives.

The consequences of climate change are not distant dystopic possibilities, they are realities that the world is facing already today.
Living in Zurich, the consequences pass us by in the form of news headlines or the unfulfilled hope of a white Christmas. However, other parts of the world are already enduring the harshest consequences of the changing climate. Floods, unbearably hot summers, irregular monsoons - this is happening today, and it is disrupting the daily lives and economic development of many communities who are least responsible for causing the change.
Let us not close our eyes to this injustice. Let us do our best to combat climate change. If you have the privilege of being able to donate to this cause, please consider doing so. Take some time to learn more about climate change and to share it with your friends and family. Let us make sure that corporations and communities all take on the responsibility of saving our climate. Because in the end, the earth will keep on turning even in the hot house scenario -  but if we want to keep our planet inhabitable for our future generations, we must take action now.

Post:
There are a lot of small actions that students can do to counter climate change. Some of them are already well known, for instance, separating trash, reducing food waste, eating less meat, saving water, using environmental-friendly hygiene products, avoiding plastic, investing in quality or recycled clothing and only turning the lights on that are actually needed. 

Traveling is another crucial topic. Before going to any place in general, we should first ask ourselves, do I really have to go (to a meeting, for example, which could also be held online)? And if I must go, how can I waste the least amount of energy to get there? Airplanes are definitely to be avoided. Using public transports instead of a car to get to university is something we should do, too, especially in Switzerland, where public transports are very developed and reliable. Nevertheless, we should use a bicycle or go on foot whenever possible and doable :-)

Digitalization is especially relevant for students. There are a lot of gadgets and online tools, like microsoft journal and onenote, that we can use to avoid wasting paper. For this matter, always try to use energy efficient tools.

Of course, supporting existing projects that help the climate and voting are also extremely important, especially young people should engage more in politics.

Climate change may feel like a global issue beyond individual control, but students in Zurich have real power to make a difference.

Moreover, getting involved in local climate groups, participating in campus sustainability events and talking about climate change with peers and friends can help spread the necessary awareness and spark collaborative action.
These are all small habits that we as students can integrate to be part of a powerful movement towards a more sustainable future.

Post:
In my opinion, one of easiest way to reduce your daily CO2 footprint is by going by bike or public transportation to university/sports/etc. instead of your own car/motorcycle. Taking the bike, besides doing something for the climate, also helps you stay healthy.

Additionally, reducing and recycling waste is important. Reducing waste can be easily done by using your own re-usable shopping bag (instead getting a new plastic bag every time) and bringing your own Tupperware if you get food to-go. TooGoodToGo is an app that helps reduce food waste of restaurants and you get a cheap and good meal. Recycling waste helps not only the environment but also saves you money in Zurich, since the blue bag costs money but bringing your glass/aluminium/paper to a "Werkstoffhof" is free.

A third way to help the environment is eating less meat. I, myself, am not a vegetarian but I have reduced my meat intake to once a week maximum. Animals need water and food and growing this food needs space. Often soja plants are used, which are planted in the South American rainforest, killing the living space for a lot of animals and decreasing the amount of trees that can convert CO2 to O2 via photosynthesis.

Supporting local, seasonal, and organic food alos reduces emissions form transporting food. And of course, recycling, composting and avoiding single-use plastics are simple but effective ways to reduce waste.

UZH has programs aimed at reducing their environmental footprint, and students can join in or eve start their own initiatives. In a world that seems to be breaking down on many different levels simultaneously, it feels redundant and repetitive to keep on preaching about the imminence and importance of climate change. The current generation of student grew up in a world and societal discourse heavily influenced by discussions about the problems arising from a changing climate. We know that the problem is the biggest challenge to have ever been faced by humans. But we also know that the size of this problem makes it extremely difficult to feel personally responsible for it. In the end, an individual will not solve it. 
Nonetheless, individual actions are key to save this planet. Not necessarily to directly stop climate change, but to create a public and common awareness for the issue. One can have a regional, seasonal and climate friendly diet, choose carbon-neutral transportation and be aware of the energy consumption of personal items. But the most important thing is: Talk about it! Bring up the issue, in conversation, in class. Climate change will only be solved if everybody cannot escape the conversation, if it is clearly communicated what is already happening as a result of a warming earth. Science needs to be discussed, needs to be more public and students, as the next generation of leaders, need to be vocal. Use your voice - talk about it!

Post:
I went two years in Eugene, Oregon, USA and their mentality on climate change was very interesting. They had bad and good habits but I will only focus on the good ones :) 

They would buy from shops that would offer local and seasonal produce. That is also possible in Zurich even with a restricted budget (Aldi, Lidl or even the local markets (bonus: some farmers sometimes offer a bouquet of aromatic plants)

The Oregonians would often go to second hand shops which is also possible here with the Heilsarmee or Facebook marketplace. 

Some of the students in the states would even compost, recycle and reuse used objects. How about melting all your old dead candle into new ones? 

I think we can all participate on our own scale, it doesn’t have to be much but it will always be more than nothing :)

Post:
Living in Olten, I often feel lucky to be surrounded by beautiful nature and a cthat values sustainabilitybut that doesn’t mean we’re doing enough. As students, we’re in a unique position: we not only shape the future through our studies, but we also influence those around us by how we live today.

I started making small changes after a classmate challenged me to track my carbon footprint for a week. It was eye-opening. I realized how often I chose convenience over sustainability (like ordering food delivery in plastic containers or flying home for short trips). Now, I try to shop second-hand, eat mostly plant-based, and take the train instead of flying whenever possible. It’s not about being perfect, but about being conscious.

If 96% of us believe climate change is a global threat, that belief should show in our daily actions. Imagine if every student brought a reusable container, reduced meat consumption just a few times a week, or spoke up when their lab or department made wasteful choices. These decisions may seem small, but multiplied across thousands of students, they have real power.

Climate action isn’t only in protests or policies, but it’s in every coffee cup we refill, every bike ride we choose, and every conversation we start.

Climate change is a global threat. This does not mean that we as individuals cannot have an impact. As students we may not have the resources to donate to charities and organizations that might directly fight climate change through various actions. However, there is a lot more we can do in our everyday lives. The most important of all hereby is to change our view on all the actions we can do in order to reduce our carbon footprint. Is it really that bad to take a ride on the bike instead of cursing about the traffic? Or does it even allow you to get some movement, free the stressed mind and might even save some time? Also, are you really missing something when eat less meat and other animal products or might you even gain new perspectives on how a meal can look like and which various possibilities of food sources we have? And the next time the letter for elections and votes is in your mailbox: Do you really need to be stressed out because it is too complicated and you do not have the time to get informed in order to elect the right person or vote for the best clause? Why can't it be really just enough to have a quick look on an informative website that illustrates the most important points and then you put your tick instead of forgetting about it? 
So take a second look on all the climate change actions and let's keep Earth as a place worth to live for all!

Combating climate change as an individual does not have to be hard! There are a few small changes everyone can implement in their daily life.
For example: Reduce the amount of power you use! Instead of heating up your place, choose to wear another layer of clothes. Instead of turning on the AC or a ventilator at home, choose to keep your place cool by closing the blinds. Don't use the AC in your car, open the windows. Stop using the elevator, instead use the stairs. 
Choose to buy things that can be reused instead of being thrown away after being used once. Giving away your things instead of throwing them in the trash and buying second hand will also make a difference. Eating more local food, vegetables and fruits and throwing away less food is also a great change to make.
Some of these changes are easier implemented than others. However, most of these changes will benefit you as well! You will save money and live healthier, so it's a win-win.

Better to have a piece of clothing that is two times more expensive but lasts five times as long, because it will usually be cheaper in the long run. The same logic goes for any type of household appliance or electronics: cellphones laptops and co. require lots of rare-earth metals which are really hard to extract, are generally toxic and their production harms the environment. The main focus when buying any type of electronics should be on their durability and reliability.

Post:
As students living and studying in Zürich we have a unique position, surrounded my exceptional public transport, cutting edge research institutions and culture with a large drive to become sustainable. We believe our stance should reciprocate this and a few meaningful yet small changes to our everyday choices can create impact.
1. Choose shared mobility
-- Use trams, buses or S-Bahn for instead of car-rides, whenever possible
-- If the route allows, cycle or walk to campus, the city has infrastructure which makes it both safe and enjoyable
2. Reduce and optimize energy use at home
– Unplug chargers and appliances when not in use, and switch to LED bulbs—your landlord (or WG-mates) will thank you for the lower electricity bills too.
– Investigate green-energy tariffs; many Swiss suppliers offer plans sourced 100% from renewables. Align your subscriptions with providers committed to phasing out fossil fuels.
3. Rethink your diet
– Incorporate more plant-based meals into your week: a simple “Meat-free Monday” is a classic starting point.
– Shop at weekly farmers’ markets—supporting local producers reduces transport-related emissions and fosters community connections.
4. Embrace the circular economy
– Opt for second-hand textbooks, clothes and furniture via Ricardo, Tutti or local flea markets.
– Recycle correctly: Zurich’s blue paper-and-cardboard bins, yellow PET collection points and organic-waste containers are all part of a highly efficient system—learn your neighborhood’s schedule!
5. Get involved beyond your own footprint
– Join campus sustainability initiatives (ETH’s Energy Science Center or UZH’s Green Campus, for instance) to collaborate on renewable-energy research or tree-planting campaigns.
– Raise awareness among your peers: organize a film screening, lead a discussion group or simply share practical tips over coffee.

Combatting climate change isn’t about perfection, but progress. By embedding small, daily choices into our routines—whether that’s swapping a Lyft for a tram ride or choosing reusable over single-use—we collectively send a powerful signal: students in Zurich care deeply about their planet’s future, and we’re ready to act.

Post: The difficulty in fighting climate change seems to be that we are fighting the whole world at once. We are fighting industries that make their profits from unsustainable products. We are fighting governments that try to achieve wealth in countries where people suffer from terrible standards of living. But most of all, we are fighting people who understandably do not want to believe that the whole world will change for the worse in consequence to their lives changing for the better. For this reason I believe that the best we can do is stay humble and consume less in every aspect of our lives. Opting for low-carbon transportation: Choose to walk or take the tram instead of driving a private car; Saving Energy: Turn off lights and unplug electronics when leaving a room...

Start today. Start now. Turn these small actions into lasting habits. Don't wait for a crisis to act!

- avoid flying

- reduce one's meat and diary consumption, eventually become vegetarian/vegan oreven advocate for plant-based universities. 
The potential  influence of student's acts to combat climate change is not to be neglected as historically universities have been places where societal changes often begins.

Post:
Each of us can do many different things to help combat climate change to some degree. While many people making small changes in their everyday lives can make a difference too, I think it is far more important, that we become conscious of the main culprits, which are for example most huge corporations (and not you or me taking an airplane once a year). 
A topic that is very important to me, is online shopping, especially on platforms like Temu or Shein. These are horrific contributors to not only the destruction of our planet, but also the exploitation of workers, not to speak of the toxicity of the chemicals in their unregulated products. People claiming to care even a bit about the environment, while shopping on such platforms, are extremely hypocritical. And seeing how 96% believe climate change to be an important topic, while Temu sales are only rising further, I would say that includes a pretty big part of those people as well. 
But not only these online platforms are a problem. Most clothing retailers for example, have massively lowered the quality of their products over the last few years, while going for more and more mass production. Microplastic for example has been a huge concern for quite some time and it is only getting worse, with even the majority of clothes being made out of plastic nowadays. 
So my appeal to all fellow students would be to stop supporting corporations like Temu, Shien, etc. and try to steer away from unnecessary mass consumption of low quality mass produced products altogether.

Post: Combating climate change in our daily lives starts with small things. Of course it would have a bigger impact to just stop doing things that are highly polluting the planet, like some extraction of minerals, using cars, making factories ecological, etc., but those things are much more difficult to implement, since they have also other impacts and many people are involved. So what can we do in our daily lives? A lot of people forget that if we all do small things to help the planet, in the end it adds up and transforms into big things that help the planet. We can start by recycling every waste that can be recycled, not wasting water by letting the tap open when brushing teeth, turning off lights that are not needed, not being part of this overconsumption trend that everyone is following (why buy 20 new clothes when you already have enough?) and so using things until you really cannot use them anymore. We can buy second hand when it works well for us, not waste food, start eating less meat since its production is also highly polluting, use more public transport than our own car. And there are more and more things that can be done. Start small, and you’ll get big results! If everyone does this, imagine the impact that it can have. What if you’re the only one missing? ;)

Post:
I think there are to realistic avenues we as students can contribute to combatting climate science.
First, there is just to alter personal habits. For example to consume less, to think twice if a purchase is really necessary and  reuse and recycle as much as possible or even already be minful of you power and heating consumption. It does not have to be a radical change but can also be an incremental process. While donating would also be possible, I recognize that as a student (especially in Zürich) we may not be in a financial position to do that. This also holds for changes concerning local and bio products. While it would be better to look at the origin and production standarts for things we buy, it might just not be financially possible. That said, I do think it to be beneficial (both for the environment and for me personally) to spend a bit more for higher quality products that might even be locally produced and that last longer and thus generate less waste.
Secondly, It's through the choice of focus for your studies and your future work. You can make a conscious decision to do research or work in a field which actively tries to improve efficiency and carbon equivalent emissions and thus contribute to combatting climate change. I think this avenue is the most impactful we can choose as students, as  it not only furthers our understanding and tools but also shapes public opinion, which might be one of the biggest factors in solving this problem.

Post: Climate change is something that will impact all lives on earth, regardless of nationality, regardless of species. While addressing the responsibility of firms and states remains an imperative and highly relevant issue, individual changes can effectively contribute to a combined effort towards fighting climate change. Every step towards sustainability counts, and the individual choices we make in our daily lives can have an important impact not only directly, through changed behaviour and consumption, but also indirectly, through signalling the saliency of climate change through our actions, promoting environmental conciousness, and pressing politician. By adjusting our consumption we also have a powerful lever to influence these large global firms that are among the main polluters, by reducing demand for their products and requesting accountability and responsibility for harm towards the environment on a political alley. We can collectively cast repeated votes not only in the political arena, but also in everyday choices. Concretely, I would suggest drastically reducing the amount of flights individuals take per year, especially short flights that could easily be done by train or bus, reducing the amount of meat and animal products individuals consume, as they are among the largest causes for CO2 emissions. Just switching from factory farming to more "humane" sources is not a fix,  as they are about increasing well being, not reducing environmental impact. If it is possible for you to cut out meat and other animal products entirely, that is the way to go from an environmentalist perspective, but also from an animal ethics perspective. If not, reduce, and choose good sources, avoid factory farming at all costs. Finally, other consumption habits can also have an important impact, for example if you order online less frequently, in general buy less stuff, because stuff needs to be manufactured and shipped around the world, and also take care of what you own. Don't treat things with less care because they are cheap and readily available, always try to maximize the lifespan of anything you buy. Maybe choose better quality products from the get-go, if your budget allows it, that you never even have to face the sentiment of "Oh, this was cheap, it doesn't really matter if it breaks". Also avoid going into sales looking for bargains to be made, like is common on promotional campaigns such as black friday. Buy what you need, not what is currently cheaper than usually. Generally, I feel most have a good understanding of what is good and what is bad for the environment, the question is more about who should bare the responsibility. I don't think it's helpful to shift it either way, but rather to focus on maximized sustainability from everyone. If the world becomes uninhabitable, no one cares about I told you so, so let's make sure we can avoid an uninhabitable world.

Post:
As (probably somewhat affluent) people living in central europe, we'll be among the ones least affected by climate change. Still our outlook doesn't look good. And as if that wasn't enough: the outlook for the next couple of generations looks even worse.
Climate change is one of the main examples for how the normality we inhabit is in many ways unacceptable. How the life we're used to is currently tied to a huge amount of present, past and future suffering and destruction. This is not a happy thought.

Shortly after the US-elections of 2024, the CEO of Partners In Health wrote in their newsletter about hopelessness and staying motivated to try to better things. She said that PIH feels as motivated as ever because they know the following two things to be true:
1. "Action is the antidote to despair."
2. "Bending the arc toward justice forbids us the luxury of being pessimistic on behalf of those who can't afford to loose hope."
I quite like this because it shows two facets of altruism. 1. A sense of empowerment. 2. A sense of responsibility (in the 'duty' sense, not in the 'blame' sense). To me this is motivating.

Yet, we are students. And as such, don't we usually lack the time and money to spend on good causes? There are all the everyday choices we make that strongly influence our personal contribution to the problem (what do I eat, what transportation do I use, how much do I buy) and there are the votes we cast. And all these things are already something. We can 'do our part'. But a lingering feeling remains that this won't solve the problem; at no time will everybody be doing their part and not at all times will we be doing our part. Luckily there is more we can do:
- Since the Swiss currency is so strong, I think we should not underestimate the impact our donations can have. What looks like a small sum to us might look larger in another country.
- As students we are still very much in the process of choosing the skills we want to acquire, the field we want to work in etc. All these choices might not really have any impact on the external world right now, but they could have a huge impact on the influence we have on the world over the course of our lives.
- Maybe we can already get a little more involved in politics after all. We don't need to be Nationalrat to collect signatures or do campaigning.

If only every second person in this world adds a drop of water into a an empty pool, it eventually will be full. Sure it would be more efficient if few people came and dumped in a big bucket of water, but with the waterdrops the pool still can be filled.
As we have a limited amount of time to fix climate change, at least to some extent, buckets would be more efficient, but even a pool filled with a little water is something.
Zurich is a huge city, which makes it fairly easy to change some things, without making a big effort. Second of all, all mensas at UZH offer a great vegan and vegetarian menus and there are several restaurants all over Zurich, which cook without meat. So one can experience cheap and nutritous meat and still contribute something positive to climate change. Post:
How can you and other students in Zurich contribute to combating climate change in their daily lives?

The best decision from a game-theoretic perspective is not always the one that is best for everyone, or for the climate. So it is not very feasible to go and live in a little tiny-house, with ones own garden, living in an entirely self-sustainable way. To study requires a home close to the university, or access to public transport, as well as digital devices etc. But I guess there are at least some actions that reduce our footprint: Things like bringing one's own cup of coffee, or limiting usage of computing ressources (LLM's...), sorting the trash and taking less flights. These will at least have some minor impact. However I think that our biggest contribution to climate could be attained in developing technologies or materials that use less resources or are more sustainable. I think that we need good global regulations and laws.

I think that ideally there should be minimum requirements that products should fulfill by law to be somewhat sustainable. But then again no country wants to have a disadvantage. So the next best option is (or would be) to carefully choose which products we buy.

Post: The Climate change problem is often framed as a whole-planet collective action problem, that is not soluble within our available temporal window until a certain civilizational implosion or the collapse of biodiversity. Where we think that whatever we do, the problem isn't solved unless everyone does the same. Well realistically speaking about the climate change problem, comparing different scales (bigger and smaller organizations, institutions, populations, etc.) different problems are faced. Anyhow, when asking myself what I as a student of Zurich can do, I like to think of what skills humans had, which survived natural selection: humanity, as in having empathy to the ones around us and wanting to survive with them, as in being creative about problems, and listening to my gut feeling about what I should and should not do. Post:
In our daily lives it might feel hard to "do your part" in combating climate change. Living on a tight budget and high amounts of stress are the biggest hurdles. Choosing climate friendly products, i.e. without plastic packaging or of organic quality can seem hard if that would make the price double. Instead I'd argue that as students we are learning for the life we will be living after uni as well. Hence, general life style choices such as trying a vegetarian or even plant based diet is also a feasible option that can even be cheaper than not doing it. Additionally, one can choose to shop 2nd hand and always carry an extra tote bag and a small cutlery set in their school bag to avoid having to use single-use plastics. This can be combined with an active exchange with other students, join a club related to climate issues, go on a protest.

To summarise, in my opinion the average student in Zurich can contribute to combat climate change by starting to change habits that have a negative effect on the environment, to connect with peers to learn about other ideas on what to do and to process the mental load that comes with the weight of climate change on our outlook on the future. 

One can change their habits but together we can change the options we are given, just think of the recent rice of vegan products in supermarkets!

I do believe that most of us can do small changes in our lives - use trains instead of motorbikes or cars, buy packaging free food, however I think that most of these miss the big picture. A lot of positive change can come from increased political activity in our daily lives - be it on family, local or national level. If we have a neighbor that needs new heating, I think we should pitch in and say we are willing to help him choose a heatpump, solar, or eco friendly other solution. We should also demand better circular economy for glass, electronics repairability, changes to building codes that lower the cost of construction and make it more eco friendly such as building with raw stone of which there is inexhaustible supply in Switzerland. I think it is important to remember that while everyone has moral obligation to mitigate climate change, successfully persuading more people and industries to better solutions will have much more impact than isolated individual level changes, as such learning how to be better communicator is I think one of the most impactful ways we can bring about bigger change.

Post:
I believe global warming is an important problem for our society, and to solve it, we must cooperate across the planet. I believe the best way to do this in an ideal world would be to set emission targets for every country around the world and follow a certain plan. However, watching political developments around the world, I do not think this will happen.

Instead, I believe we should do our best to make being climate-friendly as economically feasible as possible. In recent years, we have seen some amazing advances in solar panel technology and other renewable sources that can make solar power even cheaper than traditional fossil fuels in certain conditions, and I fully hope that as technology progresses, this will become a standard in many other fields as well. Then, transitioning to a more climate-friendly society will not be dictated by political regimes, but by pure economic incentive, which seems much more realistic to me.

As for how we can help the best as a society, I'd say to not be wasteful and to educate ourselves about the topic. And of course, to support companies and motivated people who are willing to conduct research in this area, bringing us ever closer to a brighter tomorrow!

Since a lot of emissions are not within our direct control it is vitally important to participate in every election and push for political changes. Additionally it's important to cut back on consumption contributing a lot to climate change but only little to our own life quality. Here the preferences are of course individual. Post:
On an individual level, I think there are several domains in which our choices can have a tangible effect on combating climate change, especially if these choices are adopted by the general population and not just a handful of people.

The first, and the likely easiest domain where one can make a difference in Switzerland, is the consumer behaviour. This includes things like adjusting behaviour related to fashion, food, transport etc. For instance, instead of supporting a polluting fashion industry with opaque supply chains and dubious labour practices, we could buy second hand clothes, or clothes manufactured ethically from Europe. Similarly, buying local produce that is in season rather than produce shipped from the other corner of the globe while also avoiding food waste is not only healthy but also good for the environment. For transport, opting for trains and public transport rather (at least in Europe) than planes and cars would also be a good step forward. 

Another domain that I think is important to consider in order to combat climate change is politics. While it is true that individuals should be aware of their consumer behaviour, it is also well known that private companies are by far the largest pollutors. In my opinion, companies should be held accountable for their emissions and general environmental impact. Currently, due to an inconsistent set of regulations with loopholes, grey areas and ambiguous requirements (not only in Switzerland but also the EU), many companies are likely not doing enough to combat climate change. As consumers but also as citizens, we have the right to require our politicians to pass laws that regulate the activities of companies such that their impact on the environment is either offset through taxes or through social programs. Luckily in Switzerland, citizen invoked referendums have a lot of weight on decision making which is why getting involved in groups or organizations that promote the regularization of companies and in general the fight against climate change is in my opinion more effective than individual action. 

Additional to the point made above, while individual consumer choices can help to an extent (and are by far the most comfortable way of contributing and feeling good about yourself for tackling climate change), being socially involved is probably the most important contribution you can have. In my opinion, the individualistic convenience culture that we live in has the insidious side effect that it makes people think that climate change is also a matter of individual action, conveniently fixable by only adjusting our consumer practices. In reality, at least in my opinion, climate change was never an individual isssue and it cannot be fixed by individuals, it can only by fixed with social inititiatives and with the engagement of communities.

Post:
To be clear, there are not so many things we can do on individual basis, and I find it, generally, a wrong focus, since the main contributors to climate change are still big firms, e.g. state-controlled energy companies or oil giants. So the first thing we should start with is always making them responsible for the damage they caused to the planet.
Secondly, if we return to the focus on individual contributions, there are many good calculators online, showing clearly what we have to do to reduce our emissions. And the main point would be (despite what many would think first like flying) is accepting vegetarian or vegan diet - that step alone could reduce your carbon footprint by 25-30%.
On the second place by the impact would be individual cars and especially everyday commute by car. As long as people use cars for commute, it would be almost impossible to bring a city like Zürich to zero emissions goal it has set for 2050.
There are many other measures, but they're negligible in proportion to two aforementioned ones.

People might blame it on 'luck', 'just a phase the Earth is going to' or 'a natural process humans have nothing to do with', but it's hard to ignore the fact that the environment we live in is drastically changing, which consequently affects our lives too. But if people are presented with a somehow established "climate friendlier" choice I think people would be more likely to choose it. This does not mean that they can choose an alternative, that is more harmful to the climate, it just suggests the lesser harmful one. The big issue with all of this is: How do we know that choices presented are the less climate impactful ones? And how do they interact with other choices? Will there be a rebound-effect? etc.. Post: Climate change is a global threat that needs our immediate attention. I know it seems like this topic is being spoken about often and most people think it's the big companies or celebrities with private jets who can bring about real change by altering their lifestyles. But if everyone thinks like this we will go nowhere. Just doing your part, however big or small that may be, has a compounding effect. Your actions might inspire others around you to be more mindful who will in turn inspire others and so on. Notwithstanding this influence chain, just doing your part gives you a clean conscience. That being said, how can one contribute to combatting climate change? As students, we already contribute by mostly using public transport and biking to most places (A good thing owing private vehicles are expensive! Not to mention the traffic!) Little things like eliminating plastic as much as possible from our lives could make a significant impact as it reduces the demand and hence profit minded companies will try to steer away from it. I used to be a big user of plastic - Tupperwares, storage boxes, plastic covers to carry things. I believe that each one of us needs to be more aware of the use of any tool, technological or otherwise, in order to better understand the impact it can have in the long term and added to the population as whole. At this time in history, scientific development is stronger than ever, but the continuous desire to improve our lives only makes future lives worse and worse. Climate change is an issue that may not affect us during our individual lifetimes, but could heavily influence the lives of those who will follow us. 

I am in favour of progress, but I am even more in favour of the conscientious use of the means we have at our disposal, so that each of us can assess whether it is worth it or not. My advice is to think about this not by seeing ourselves as individuals in out own right, but as part of a world and a species that cannot move forward if everyone continues to think only of their own good. 

I am not the kind of person who would demonstrate in the streets to hope for a revolution in a specific area, such as climate change; I am the kind of person who would focus on raising the individual's awareness and developing critical and ethical thinking, which does not only think of the good of oneself, but of all living beings indiscriminately.
